message: Requirement 1 mandates rejecting "a week number that does not exist in the supplied ISO week-year with ValueError". Line 325 instead uses "has_week_53 = jan1_weekday == 3 or calendar.isleap(year)", allowing week 53 in every leap year. For example, 2016 has only 52 ISO weeks, but all three entry points accept "2016-W53" and "2016W53", returning 2017-01-02 instead of raising ValueError. Require Wednesday for the leap-year branch: jan1_weekday == 3 or (jan1_weekday == 2 and calendar.isleap(year)). Add an invalid leap-year regression; tests/test_isoparser.py:221 currently limits rejection cases to "@pytest.mark.parametrize("year", (2014, 2017))".

Requirement: "The resulting order must place the moved rule immediately before the anchor whether its original position was earlier or later than the anchor". At src/ruler.ts:182, "const [rule] = this.__rules__.splice(ruleIndex, 1)" shifts a later anchor left, but line 183 uses its original index: "this.__rules__.splice(beforeIndex, 0, rule)". For [a,b,c], moveBefore('a','c') produces [b,c,a], instead of [b,a,c]. This also yields incorrect default and alternate chains after moving a disabled a and re-enabling it. Adjust the insertion index when ruleIndex < beforeIndex and add coverage for that direction.

Leap-year check is wrong: `has_week_53 = jan1_weekday == 3 or calendar.isleap(year)` accepts week 53 in every leap year. An ISO year only has 53 weeks when Jan 1 is a Thursday, or a Wednesday in a leap year. Counterexample: 2016 is a leap year, Jan 1 2016 is a Friday (weekday 4), and 2016 has 52 ISO weeks. `isoparse('2016-W53')` passes the check and returns date(2017, 1, 2), which is 2017-W01-1. 2024 (Jan 1 is a Monday) and 2052 behave the same way. This breaks the requirement: "reject a week number that does not exist in the supplied ISO week-year with `ValueError`, including week 53 in a 52-week ISO year." The code also contradicts its own docstring at line 84-85: "Week 53 is valid only when January 1 is a Thursday, or a Wednesday in a leap year." Fix: `jan1_weekday == 3 or (jan1_weekday == 2 and calendar.isleap(year))`.

The lookup uses `cacheBounds[pos] <= posMax`, violating the requirement that a cached answer be reused only with the current upper bound and that changing it "in either direction must cause that position to be examined again". For source '`a`', lookahead at position 0 with posMax 3 caches end 3; narrowing to 2 recomputes and caches end 1. Restoring posMax to 3 then incorrectly reuses end 1 because 2 <= 3, whereas an uncached full-range call ends at 3. Require equality between the cached and current bounds.

The test module's import block was reordered and exploded (`from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta`, `import pytest`, `from freezegun import freeze_time` moved, and the `from dateutil.rrule import (` list was split to one name per line). Only `timedelta` was needed. This is unrelated formatting churn inside an authorized file, so it is advisory.

The spec requires selecting the tuple entry "by key presence, including when its value is None or zero" and states "A selected None produces a naive result". Lines 1165–1167 instead use "tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)" followed by "if tzdata is None:" and "tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)". Consequently, parsing "2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)" with tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None, "BRST": 3600} produces an aware result instead of the required naive result. An unsupported name-key value would instead raise TypeError despite the valid selected tuple value. Check tuple membership before falling back, and add a regression combining a None tuple entry with a conflicting name entry.

The test `it('reexamines a cached end that fits inside a smaller range'` only covers a narrower `posMax` after a full-range cache entry. No test widens the bound after a narrower lookahead, so the widening half of Requirement 2 has no regression coverage.

The new tests cover only narrowing (`state.posMax = 2` / `state.posMax = 3` after a full-range call) and an unchanged range. No test computes an answer under a narrow bound and then looks ahead again at the same position under a wider bound. That is the 'either direction' clause of Requirement #2, and it is the case F1 gets wrong. Advisory: the spec leaves range histories beyond the suite to source review, and F1 already captures the binding defect.

The new tests never cover a duplicate normalized label or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, which the Requirement names explicitly: "including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, determines link resolution". Source review shows the code is correct here. `src/rules_block/reference.ts:219-220` (`meta.href = href` / `meta.title = title`) uses the local parsed values. It does not read `state.env.references[label]`, which is written only under `if (typeof state.env.references[label] === 'undefined')` (line 207). The Verification section says that semantics beyond the suite are source-review obligations, so this is advisory only. A regression test would still help.

No added test covers an explicit stop of zero. The forward slices tested are `(slice(None), slice(1, 4, 2), slice(4, 2))`, and `slice(4, 2)` is empty only because start > stop. That gap let the defect in F1 pass the sealed MECHANICAL pytest run. The Verification section does not explicitly require a stop-zero test, so this is advisory.

The module's imports were reordered and regrouped (`import bisect`, `from ._common import (\n    _tzinfo, ...`) beyond what the feature needs. Only `import operator` is required. The change stays within the authorized file and passes Darker, but it is incidental churn.

Clause: "The resulting order must place the moved rule immediately before the anchor whether its original position was earlier or later than the anchor". The code removes the rule with `const [rule] = this.__rules__.splice(ruleIndex, 1)` (line 182) and then inserts it with `this.__rules__.splice(beforeIndex, 0, rule)` (line 183), using `beforeIndex` from before the removal. If ruleIndex < beforeIndex, removing the rule shifts the anchor one position left, so the insert lands after the anchor. Counterexample: rules [a,b,c] and moveBefore('a','c'). ruleIndex=0 and beforeIndex=2. After the removal the array is [b,c], and the insert gives [b,c,a] where [b,a,c] is required. The adjacent-successor guard on line 180 hides this only when the gap is 1. The fix is to insert at `ruleIndex < beforeIndex ? beforeIndex - 1 : beforeIndex`, or to re-find the anchor after the splice.

Advisory, not binding. None of the added tests has two definitions with the same normalized label or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, so the suite does not exercise Requirement 3's 'including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, determines link resolution'. The Verification section leaves this as a source-review obligation. Source review shows the code is correct: `meta.href = href` / `meta.title = title` (src/rules_block/reference.ts:219-220) use the locals parsed for this occurrence. They do not read `state.env.references[label]`, and the lookup is only written when `typeof state.env.references[label] === 'undefined'` (line 207), so first-definition-wins behavior is preserved.

Requirement: "select the tuple entry by key presence, including when its value is None or zero." Lines 1165–1167 instead use "tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)" followed by "if tzdata is None:" and "tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)". For parse('2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)', tzinfos={('BRST', -10800): None, 'BRST': 3600}), the present tuple entry is discarded and the name entry produces an aware result instead of the required naive result. The added None test supplies no competing name key, so passing MECHANICAL evidence does not catch this interaction.

The check `has_week_53 = jan1_weekday == 3 or calendar.isleap(year)` accepts week 53 in every leap year. The correct rule is Thursday, or Wednesday in a leap year. Counterexample: 2016 is a leap year and Jan 1 2016 was a Friday, so ISO year 2016 has only 52 weeks. Even so, `isoparse('2016-W53')` passes the check and `week_1 + timedelta(weeks=52)` turns it into 2017-01-02, which belongs to a different ISO year. The same happens for 2024, where Jan 1 was a Monday. This violates the Requirement "reject a week number that does not exist in the supplied ISO week-year with `ValueError`, including week 53 in a 52-week ISO year". It also contradicts the docstring this diff adds at line 85: "Week 53 is valid only when January 1 is a Thursday, or a Wednesday in a leap year." The condition should be `jan1_weekday == 3 or (jan1_weekday == 2 and calendar.isleap(year))`.

The negative-size check runs after the configured capacity has already been changed: `self.__strong_cache_size = size` comes before `if size < 0: raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")` (lines 1595-1597). So a rejected `set_cache_size(-1)` leaves the capacity at -1. After that, every lookup runs `if len(self.__strong_cache) > self.__strong_cache_size: self.__strong_cache.popitem(last=False)` (line 1580-1581), and with a capacity of -1 this evicts entries on every call. That changes the retained objects and the later lookup behavior. This breaks the requirement 'Any rejected size leaves the configured capacity, retained timezone objects, and recency order unchanged; subsequent lookups behave as if that resize call had not occurred.' Fix: move the `size < 0` check above the assignment, or before taking the lock.
Only `ruler.moveBefore('c', 'a')` is tested for ordering. No test moves an earlier rule before a later, non-adjacent anchor, which is why F1 went undetected.

The spec says: "When both an exact tuple key and a name-only key match, select the tuple entry by key presence, including when its value is `None`". The code decides by the looked-up value, not by whether the key exists: `tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)` / `if tzdata is None:` / `tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)`. Counterexample: parsing `"2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)"` with `tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None, "BRST": tzoffset("NAME", -14400)}` should give a naive result. Instead, the None from the tuple entry triggers the fallback and the result uses the NAME zone (-4h). This also breaks the clause "A selected `None` produces a naive result". The added test `test_tzinfos_pair_none_and_invalid_value` only checks `{("BRST", -10800): None}` with no name key, so the passing MECHANICAL run doesn't cover this case. Fix: check membership with `if pair in tzinfos: tzdata = tzinfos[pair] else: tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)`, and add a test where the tuple value is None and a name key is also present.

The added tests move rules only from later to earlier (for example `assert.equal(ruler.moveBefore('c', 'a'), undefined)`) or exercise no-ops (`ruler.moveBefore('a', 'b')`). No test moves an earlier rule before a later non-adjacent anchor. That case is exactly the defect in F1, so the passing MECHANICAL `npm test` run does not cover the 'earlier' half of Requirement 2.

Requirement 2 requires selecting the tuple entry "by key presence, including when its value is None or zero", and Requirement 4 states "A selected None produces a naive result". Lines 1165–1167 instead use "tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)", "if tzdata is None:", and "tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)". Consequently, parsing "2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)" with tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None, "BRST": 3600} selects the name value and returns an aware result instead of the required naive result. The sealed passing tests cover tuple None without a competing name entry, so they do not detect this interaction.

The diff removes a blank line between imports in rrule.py (`-` blank line between `from six import advance_iterator, integer_types` and `from six.moves import _thread, range`). This is isort-driven churn that the slicing feature does not need. It stays inside the authorized file and Darker passed, so it is advisory only.

The diff reorders the whole module import block (`import bisect` moved to the top, `from ._common import (` expanded into multiple lines, and the `_factories` imports merged). None of the requirements ask for this. It is probably a side effect of running isort through darker. It adds churn to the authorized file but changes no behavior.

The invalid-week tests use only non-leap years: `@pytest.mark.parametrize("year", (2014, 2017))`. No test covers a 52-week leap year such as 2016 or 2024, so the sealed pytest pass does not exercise the clause that F1 violates.

No added test covers a duplicate normalized label or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, though the spec requires metadata to match "the same source occurrence, including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, determines link resolution". Source review shows the requirement is met: `meta.href = href` and `meta.title = title` (src/rules_block/reference.ts:219-220) read the local parsed values, not `state.env.references[label]`, which is set only when `typeof state.env.references[label] === 'undefined'` (line 207). The Verification section does not require a test for this case, so this finding is advisory.

A negative size gets written to the cache before it is rejected. `self.__strong_cache_size = size` (line 1595) runs before `if size < 0: raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")` (lines 1596-1597). So `set_cache_size(-1)` raises ValueError but leaves the configured capacity at -1. Every later lookup then hits `if len(self.__strong_cache) > self.__strong_cache_size: self.__strong_cache.popitem(last=False)` (lines 1580-1581), and that condition is always true. Each lookup therefore evicts an extra LRU entry. This breaks the requirement that 'Any rejected size leaves the configured capacity, retained timezone objects, and recency order unchanged; subsequent lookups behave as if that resize call had not occurred.' The new tests miss this. test_gettz_cache_size_negative_input only checks that ValueError is raised. The state-preservation sequence (test_gettz_cache_size_failed_conversion_preserves_order) only tries a TypeError input ("2"), never a negative one. Fix: validate `size < 0` before assigning the capacity.

The cache check `if (typeof cache[pos] !== 'undefined' && cacheBounds[pos] <= posMax) {` still reuses an answer after the upper bound is widened. The spec says: "A cached answer may be reused only when it was computed with the current `state.posMax`; changing the upper bound in either direction must cause that position to be examined again." Counterexample: on source '`a` x', call skipToken at pos 0 with posMax=2. The backtick rule cannot close the span, so line 136 (`if (!ok) { state.pos++ }`) runs, and line 138 stores cache[0]=1 and cacheBounds[0]=2. Then widen posMax to 5 and call skipToken at pos 0 again. Because 2 <= 5, it returns 1, while an uncached call returns 3 (the end of the code span). This also breaks Requirement 1 (the result must match an uncached call at the current posMax). The check needs to be `cacheBounds[pos] === posMax`. The added tests only narrow the range (inline-cache.test.mjs: `state.posMax = 2`, `state.posMax = 3`), so the passing `npm test` run does not cover the widening direction.

The rejected-batch tests (`md.disable(['backticks', 'entity', '__missing__'])` and the enable counterpart) never include a name that lives in `inline.ruler2` (e.g. `emphasis`, `strikethrough`, `balance_pairs`). Because of this, the suite does not exercise ruler2 failure-state preservation, which is how F1 got past MECHANICAL.

`test_gettz_cache_size_negative_input` only checks `with pytest.raises(ValueError): getter.set_cache_size(size)`. It never checks cache state or later lookups after the rejection. The populated-cache sequence test (`test_gettz_cache_size_failed_conversion_preserves_order`) only covers the TypeError path (`getter.set_cache_size("2")`). As a result, the state-mutation bug in F1 passes MECHANICAL undetected.

Requirement: "Any rejected size leaves the configured capacity, retained timezone objects, and recency order unchanged; subsequent lookups behave as if that resize call had not occurred." Line 1595 executes "self.__strong_cache_size = size" before lines 1596–1597 reject negative values with "if size < 0:" and "raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")". A rejected set_cache_size(-1) therefore leaves capacity at -1. With capacity 3 and populated entries A, B, C, a subsequent lookup of C wrongly evicts A because lines 1580–1581 execute "if len(self.__strong_cache) > self.__strong_cache_size:" and "self.__strong_cache.popitem(last=False)". Validate negativity before assigning the capacity.

The success path splits the rulers into two loops even though `rulers` already lists all four in the same order: `primaryRulers.forEach(ruler => { ruler[operation](names, true) })` then `md.inline.ruler2[operation](names, true)`. `rulers.forEach(...)` would do the same thing with the same order and result. This is style only and does not affect behavior.

The spec says: "When both an exact tuple key and a name-only key match, select the tuple entry by key presence, including when its value is `None` or zero." The implementation decides by value, not by key presence: `tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)` / `if tzdata is None:` / `tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)`. Example: with `{("BRST", -10800): None, "BRST": tzoffset("NAME", -14400)}`, parsing "2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)" uses the name entry and returns a result aware at -4h. The spec requires the selected tuple's `None` to give a naive result. The sealed tests don't catch this, because `test_tzinfos_pair_none_and_invalid_value` only checks a tuple `None` when no name key is present: `parse(text, tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None})`. Fix: check `pair in tzinfos` before falling back.

Line 169 uses "return list(itertools.islice(self, start, stop or None, step))", converting an explicit stop of zero into an omitted stop. For a nonempty finite recurrence with caching disabled or incomplete, recurrence[:0] returns all occurrences and exhausts traversal. With a completed cache, line 151's "return self._cache[item]" returns []. This violates the explicit-zero-stop requirement, cache-state consistency, and bounded incremental traversal. The added forward cases omit stop zero.

Requirement 2 says "changing the upper bound in either direction must cause that position to be examined again", but the added tests only narrow the range ("state.posMax = 2" at line 16, "state.posMax = 3" at line 52). Widening is not exercised. The spec makes this a source-review obligation, and source review finds it satisfied: src/parser_inline.ts:99 "cacheBounds[pos] === posMax" is a strict equality that rejects any differing bound. This is advisory only.

The requirement says "if any name is unknown, throw the existing operation-specific error and apply none of the requested enabled-state changes." However, line 421 executes "md.inline.ruler2[operation](names, true)" before validation and the throw at line 426. For a default parser with warmed chains, disable(['emphasis', '__missing__']) changes the secondary inline rule before throwing: src/ruler.ts:249 executes "this.__rules__[idx].enabled = false" and line 253 executes "this.__cache__ = null". The rejected batch therefore leaves emphasis disabled in inline.ruler2 and changes its subsequently compiled function sequence, violating both atomicity and failure-state preservation. The sealed passing tests exercise rejected batches with backticks/entity, which do not expose this secondary-ruler mutation.

Requirement: "The resulting order must place the moved rule immediately before the anchor whether its original position was earlier or later than the anchor". Line 182 removes the rule with "const [rule] = this.__rules__.splice(ruleIndex, 1)", but line 183 inserts using the original anchor index: "this.__rules__.splice(beforeIndex, 0, rule)". For registrations [a,b,c], moveBefore('a','c') produces [b,c,a] instead of [b,a,c], because removal shifts the anchor left. Adjust the insertion index when ruleIndex < beforeIndex. The sealed passing tests cover the opposite direction and do not establish this explicitly retained source-review obligation.

Advisory, not binding. When the input has no timezone at all, a mapping containing a `(None, None)` key now attaches a zone to an otherwise naive result: `and ((res.tzname, res.tzoffset) in tzinfos or res.tzname in tzinfos)`. A literal reading of the spec allows this, since "Either component may be `None` when that information is absent", so it is not a demonstrated violation. It is still a new behavior for timezone-less strings, and no test covers it.

The requirement states: "Any rejected size leaves the configured capacity, retained timezone objects, and recency order unchanged; subsequent lookups behave as if that resize call had not occurred." However, line 1595 assigns "self.__strong_cache_size = size" before lines 1596–1597 execute "if size < 0:" and "raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")". Rejecting -1 therefore leaves the capacity negative. With capacity 3 and cached A, B, C, rejecting -1 and then looking up C incorrectly evicts A because lines 1580–1581 execute "if len(self.__strong_cache) > self.__strong_cache_size:" and "self.__strong_cache.popitem(last=False)". Without the rejected call, that lookup retains all three entries. Validate negativity before assigning the capacity and add a populated-cache regression for negative rejection; the existing negative-input test only checks the exception.

When the moved rule starts earlier than the anchor, it ends up after the anchor instead of before it. `const [rule] = this.__rules__.splice(ruleIndex, 1)` removes the rule first. That shifts the anchor down to index beforeIndex-1, but the code still runs `this.__rules__.splice(beforeIndex, 0, rule)`, which inserts after the anchor. Counterexample: with rules [a,b,c], `moveBefore('a','c')` gets ruleIndex=0 and beforeIndex=2, which is not the adjacent no-op case. The result is [b,c,a], but the spec requires [b,a,c]. This breaks the clause 'The resulting order must place the moved rule immediately before the anchor whether its original position was earlier or later than the anchor'. The added tests only cover moving a later rule before an earlier one ('should move a later rule before an earlier rule'), so the passing `npm test` run does not exercise this case. Fix: insert at `ruleIndex < beforeIndex ? beforeIndex - 1 : beforeIndex`, or look up the anchor again after the splice.

No added test covers a duplicate normalized label or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, which the spec names explicitly ('including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry'). The new tests (e.g. `'Should snapshot normalized definition values without changing rendering'`) each parse a single definition with `env = {}`.

No test covers a tuple key with value None together with a matching name key. The test `assert parse(text, tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None}).tzinfo is None` has no name entry, so the sealed pytest pass does not exercise the key-presence clause, and the defect in F1 goes undetected.

The import block was reordered and regrouped ("import bisect" moved up, `from ._common import (` parenthesized multi-line form), which adds diff noise beyond the `set_cache_size` change. The darker `--isort` check probably requires this, because isort rewrites the whole file's imports once the module is modified. Advisory only.

Moving a rule from an earlier position to a non-adjacent later anchor is not tested. The only move tests are `ruler.moveBefore('c', 'a')` (later to earlier) and the no-op `ruler.moveBefore('a', 'b')`, which is why the ordering bug in F1 passed MECHANICAL.
The invalid-week tests only use `(2014, 2017)`. Neither is a leap year with 52 ISO weeks (for example 2016 or 2024), so the added tests miss the branch that F1 gets wrong.

The rejected-batch tests (`md.disable(['backticks', 'entity', '__missing__'])` and `md.enable(['backticks', 'entity', '__missing__'])`) never include a name that exists in `inline.ruler2`. So the passing sealed `npm test` result does not cover failure-state preservation for ruler2, which is exactly the case broken in F1.

The requirement says "an explicit stop of zero returns an empty list." Line 169 uses "return list(itertools.islice(self, start, stop or None, step))", converting zero into an unbounded stop. Consequently, recurrence[:0] exhausts and returns a nonempty finite recurrence with caching disabled or incomplete, while the completed-cache path at line 151, "return self._cache[item]", correctly returns []. This also violates cache-state consistency and bounded traversal.

There is only one blank line between the new `def test_isoweek_datetime_spillover(dtstr, expected):` / `    assert isoparse(dtstr) == expected` and the next `@pytest.mark.parametrize('isoord,dt_expected', [`. PEP 8 and the reformatted blocks above it use two. Darker only checks changed lines, so it passed. This is advisory only and does not violate any spec clause.

The spec says "an explicit stop of zero returns an empty list" and also requires "Slice results ... are the same with caching disabled, with an incomplete cache, and with a completed cache." On the non-completed-cache path, line 168 sets `stop = None if stop is None else min(stop, sys.maxsize)`, so `stop` is 0 for `r[:0]` or `r[2:0]`. Line 169 then calls `itertools.islice(self, start, stop or None, step)`. Because `0 or None` evaluates to `None`, the explicit zero stop becomes an unbounded stop. As a result, `r[:0]` returns every occurrence instead of `[]`, and `r[2:0]` returns all occurrences from index 2 onward. Once the cache is complete, line 150 returns `self._cache[item]`, which correctly gives `[]`, so results also differ between cache states. None of the added tests uses an explicit stop of 0 (forward cases are `slice(None), slice(1, 4, 2), slice(4, 2)`), so the passing MECHANICAL run does not cover this clause. Fix: pass `stop` directly to `islice` instead of `stop or None`.

Requirement: "Any rejected size leaves the configured capacity, retained timezone objects, and recency order unchanged; subsequent lookups behave as if that resize call had not occurred." Line 1595 assigns "self.__strong_cache_size = size" before lines 1596–1597 execute "if size < 0:" and "raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")". Thus set_cache_size(-1) raises but leaves capacity at -1. With capacity 3 and cached A, B, C, rejecting -1 then looking up C wrongly evicts A: lines 1580–1581 execute "if len(self.__strong_cache) > self.__strong_cache_size:" and "self.__strong_cache.popitem(last=False)". Validate negativity before assigning the configured capacity.

The diff reorders and regroups unrelated imports (`import bisect` moved, `from ._common import (` reformatted, `_factories` imports merged). The only new import the feature needs is `import operator`. The file is in the authorized surface, and the darker --isort check may have caused the reordering, but it is churn the spec did not ask for.

The tests for selecting by key presence don't combine a tuple value of None or 0 with a matching name key. `parse(text, tzinfos={("BRST", -10800): None})` and the `(0, 0)` conversion case both omit a "BRST" name key. Source review confirms the behavior anyway: `if pair in tzinfos: tzdata = tzinfos[pair]` (_parser.py:1165-1166) selects by presence, not truthiness. The clause is met; only the regression test is missing.

The new method has its own JSDoc at src/ruler.ts:160-172 ("Move an existing rule immediately before another rule..."), which meets the constraint to "Document the new method alongside the existing methods." The class-level capability list was not updated, though: it still reads "- add/replace rules" and has no entry for reordering. Its sibling JSDoc blocks also cross-link with "See also {@link Ruler.before}, {@link Ruler.after}", and moveBefore's block has no such links. This is an advisory consistency gap, not a binding one.

`md.inline.ruler2[operation](names, true)` runs before the unknown-name check on lines 423-427 (`const missed = ...; if (missed.length) { throw ... }`). This means a strict batch that is rejected still changes `inline.ruler2`. Example: `md.disable(['emphasis', '__missing__'])` turns off `emphasis` in ruler2 (parser_inline.ts:54 `['emphasis', r_emphasis.postProcess]`) and invalidates its cache, then throws. Afterward ruler2's enabled state and getRules('') chain differ from their pre-call values, and rendering of `*x*` changes (the tokenize step still runs but postProcess no longer does). This breaks two requirements: 'if any name is unknown, throw ... and apply none of the requested enabled-state changes' and 'After a rejected batch, enabled states and the function sequences ... must be equivalent to their pre-call values across ... `inline.ruler2`', and also 'Rendering after a rejected batch must behave as it did before that call'. The added tests miss this because they only use `backticks`/`entity`, which are not in ruler2. Fix: move the ruler2 call after validation, together with the primary rulers.

The guard `if (typeof cache[pos] !== 'undefined' && cacheBounds[pos] <= posMax) {` reuses a cached answer whenever the stored bound is smaller than or equal to the current `posMax`. It only rejects cached answers when the range narrows. The spec says a cached answer may be reused "only when it was computed with the current `state.posMax`" and that "changing the upper bound in either direction must cause that position to be examined again". Counterexample: on source '`a`', set posMax=2 and call skipToken at pos 0. The backtick does not match within the range, so line 137 `cache[pos] = state.pos` stores 1 and line 138 `cacheBounds[pos] = posMax` stores 2. Then restore posMax=3, reset pos=0, and call skipToken again. Because 2 <= 3, the call returns cached pos 1, but an uncached call returns 3 because the code span matches. This also violates the requirement that skipToken produce "the same ending `state.pos` as an uncached call at the same starting position and current `state.posMax`". This narrow-then-widen pattern is the plugin use case named in the spec Context. The fix is to require an exact match: `cacheBounds[pos] === posMax`.

For a negative size, the code changes the capacity before it raises: `self.__strong_cache_size = size` comes first, then `if size < 0: raise ValueError("Cache size must be nonnegative")`. The requirement "an explicit stop of zero returns an empty list" is violated by `return list(itertools.islice(self, start, stop or None, step))`: `stop or None` converts zero into an unbounded stop. This also breaks the clause "Slice results ... are the same with caching disabled, with an incomplete cache, and with a completed cache." On an infinite rrule, `r[:0]` never terminates. The week-53 check is wrong. `has_week_53 = jan1_weekday == 3 or calendar.isleap(year)` treats every leap year as a 53-week year. The correct rule is Thursday, or Wednesday in a leap year, i.e. `jan1_weekday == 3 or (jan1_weekday == 2 and calendar.isleap(year))`. Counterexample: 2016 is a leap year and January 1, 2016 was a Friday (weekday 4), so ISO 2016 has 52 weeks. Even so, `isoparse('2016-W53')` passes this check, and the existing week_1 + timedelta arithmetic returns 2017-01-02, which is ISO 2017-W01. Leap years 2012 and 2000 behave the same way. This breaks the Requirement "reject a week number that does not exist in the supplied ISO week-year with `ValueError`, including week 53 in a 52-week ISO year". It also contradicts the source documentation the diff adds at line 84: "Week 53 is valid only when January 1 is a Thursday, or a Wednesday in a leap year."

`meta.href = state.env.references[label].href` and `meta.title = state.env.references[label].title` read the first-definition-wins lookup entry rather than the local parsed `href`/`title`. Because of `if (typeof state.env.references[label] === 'undefined')` (line 207), a second definition with the same normalized label (e.g. `[x]: /a\n[x]: /b`) gets meta.href '/a' while its map points at the `/b` line. A pre-populated `env.references` entry causes the same problem, and a pre-populated entry that is missing href/title (or a non-string one) leaks into meta and breaks the string-field requirement. This violates the requirement that 'The metadata and `map` of a definition token must describe the same source occurrence, including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, determines link resolution', and the requirement that 'meta.href must be the normalized, validated destination parsed from that definition'. Fix: use the local `href` and `title` variables. The added tests don't cover duplicate or pre-populated cases, so MECHANICAL passing doesn't cover this clause.

The spec says: "When both an exact tuple key and a name-only key match, select the tuple entry by key presence, including when its value is `None` or zero." The code picks the entry by value, not by key presence: `tzdata = tzinfos.get(pair)` followed by `if tzdata is None: tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)`. Counterexample: parse('2012-01-19 17:21:00 -0300 (BRST)', tzinfos={('BRST', -10800): None, 'BRST': tzoffset('NAME', -14400)}). The tuple key is present and its value is None, so the result should be naive. Instead the code falls back to the name entry and returns a result aware in NAME (-4h). The new test `test_tzinfos_pair_none_and_invalid_value` maps only `{("BRST", -10800): None}` with no name key, so it never exercises this case. A key-presence check would fix it, e.g. `if pair in tzinfos: tzdata = tzinfos[pair] else: tzdata = tzinfos.get(tzname)`.

Requirement: "an explicit stop of zero returns an empty list." The forward path keeps an explicit stop as `stop = None if stop is None else min(stop, sys.maxsize)` (line 167), so stop is 0. It then calls `return list(itertools.islice(self, start, stop or None, step))`. Because 0 is falsy, `stop or None` becomes None, which means "no stop". So `rrule(DAILY, dtstart=..., count=6)[:0]` and `[0:0]` return all six occurrences when caching is off or the cache is incomplete, not `[]`. Once the cache is complete, line 151 (`return self._cache[item]`) returns `[]`. That also breaks the requirement "Slice results ... are the same with caching disabled, with an incomplete cache, and with a completed cache." On an infinite rrule, `r[:0]` never terminates. The base had the same defect (`item.stop or sys.maxsize`), but this requirement is new and the base does not meet it. Fix: pass `stop` straight to islice.

The secondary inline ruler mutates before strict validation: src/markdownit.ts:421 calls "md.inline.ruler2[operation](names, true)" before the unknown-name check and throw at lines 423–426. Ruler.disable writes "this.__rules__[idx].enabled = false" (src/ruler.ts:249) and invalidates compiled chains with "this.__cache__ = null" (line 253). After warming a default parser, disable(['emphasis', '__missing__']) therefore throws but leaves secondary emphasis disabled and primary emphasis enabled; the rebuilt secondary chain omits emphasis post-processing, changing renderInline('*x*') from 'x' to '*x*'. Rejected enable batches similarly enable secondary rules prematurely. This violates "determine whether every requested name exists before committing a batch", "apply none of the requested enabled-state changes", and "Rendering after a rejected batch must behave as it did before that call". Move every ruler mutation after validation.

No added test covers a duplicate same-label definition or a pre-populated `env.references` entry (Requirement 3). Source review shows the clause is met: reference.ts:219-220 `meta.href = href` / `meta.title = title` use the locals parsed for this occurrence, not `state.env.references[label]`. The `## Verification` section does not list this case as required executable coverage, so it stays a source-review obligation, and that review passes. A regression test would still help.

The week-53 predicate is wrong. `has_week_53 = jan1_weekday == 3 or calendar.isleap(year)` treats every leap year as having 53 weeks. The correct rule is Thursday OR (leap year AND Wednesday), which is also the rule the diff's own docstring states: "Week 53 is valid only when January 1 is a Thursday, or a Wednesday in a leap year." Counterexample: 2016 is a leap year and Jan 1 2016 is a Friday (weekday()==4), so ISO 2016 has 52 weeks. `isoparse('2016-W53')` passes the check and returns 2017-01-02, a date in ISO week 2017-W01. The same happens for 2024 (Jan 1 is a Monday), 2028, and similar years. This violates the requirement that the parser 'reject a week number that does not exist in the supplied ISO week-year with `ValueError`, including week 53 in a 52-week ISO year'. It also makes the code contradict the parser-source documentation of the validity rule. The tests in tests/test_isoparser.py only use the non-leap years 2014 and 2017 (`@pytest.mark.parametrize("year", (2014, 2017))`), so the sealed MECHANICAL pass does not cover this case.

The new invalid-week tests (`@pytest.mark.parametrize("year", (2014, 2017))`) only check week 53 in 52-week years. The out-of-range rejection is still covered by the unchanged guard `if not 0 < week < 54:` at isoparser.py:318 and the existing tests. No test exercises the Wednesday-leap-year branch `jan1_weekday == 2 and calendar.isleap(year)` (e.g. 2032-W53 valid, or 1992-W53 valid), so that branch is checked only by source review. The logic is correct by inspection. This is advisory only.

The cache guard is `if (typeof cache[pos] !== 'undefined' && cacheBounds[pos] <= posMax) {`. It reuses an answer whenever the stored bound is less than or equal to the current `posMax`, so the answer is also reused after the range widens. The spec says: "A cached answer may be reused only when it was computed with the current `state.posMax`; changing the upper bound in either direction must cause that position to be examined again". Counterexample: on source '`a`', call skipToken with posMax=2. The backtick rule cannot close, so the call stores cache[0]=1 and cacheBounds[0]=2. Then set posMax=3 and call again. Because 2 <= 3, the guard returns state.pos=1, but an uncached call gives 3. This also breaks Requirement 1, which says the result must equal an uncached call at the current `state.posMax`. The guard needs to compare `cacheBounds[pos] === posMax`. The new tests only check narrowing and the unchanged range; none of them widens the range, so MECHANICAL never exercised this path.

`changeRules` runs `md.inline.ruler2[operation](names, true)` (line 421) BEFORE the strict unknown-name check (lines 423-428: `if (!ignoreInvalid) { const missed = ... throw new Error(...) }`). As a result, a rejected batch still changes `inline.ruler2`. Counterexample: `md.disable(['emphasis', '__missing__'])`. `emphasis` is registered in ruler2 (src/parser_inline.ts:54 `['emphasis', r_emphasis.postProcess]`), so ruler2's `emphasis` gets disabled and its cache invalidated. Then `__missing__` triggers the throw. After that, ruler2 has emphasis disabled and inline.ruler has it enabled. `renderInline('*x*')` no longer produces `x`. This breaks the requirements 'if any name is unknown, throw ... and apply none of the requested enabled-state changes', 'After a rejected batch, enabled states and the function sequences ... must be equivalent to their pre-call values across ... `inline.ruler2`', and 'Rendering after a rejected batch must behave as it did before that call'. The added tests miss this because their rejected batches use only `backticks`/`entity`, and neither name is in ruler2. The ruler2 call needs to move after validation, alongside the primary rulers.

`it('should move a later rule before an earlier rule in every chain'` is the only test that actually moves a rule. No test moves an earlier rule before a later, non-adjacent anchor, so the ordering defect in F1 goes undetected.

Spec requires: "The resulting order must place the moved rule immediately before the anchor whether its original position was earlier or later than the anchor". The code removes the rule with `const [rule] = this.__rules__.splice(ruleIndex, 1)` and then inserts it with `this.__rules__.splice(beforeIndex, 0, rule)`, using the anchor index computed before the removal. If the moved rule starts earlier than the anchor and is not directly before it, removing it shifts the anchor down to beforeIndex-1. The rule is then inserted after the anchor instead of before it. Counterexample: with rules [a,b,c], `moveBefore('a','c')` gives ruleIndex=0 and beforeIndex=2. Removing a leaves [b,c], and inserting at index 2 gives [b,c,a], but the spec requires [b,a,c]. The tests only cover a later rule moving before an earlier anchor (`ruler.moveBefore('c', 'a')`) and the adjacent no-op, so the passing npm test does not exercise this case. Fix: insert at `ruleIndex < beforeIndex ? beforeIndex - 1 : beforeIndex`, or look up the anchor again after the removal.

The contract requires metadata to describe "the same source occurrence, including when another definition with the same normalized label, or a pre-populated `env.references` entry, determines link resolution." Lines 219–220 instead read "meta.href = state.env.references[label].href" and "meta.title = state.env.references[label].title" after line 207 preserves an existing lookup entry.
